**The Weight of a Single Word**

There’s a moment, just before dawn, when the world holds its breath. The air is thick with the kind of silence that isn’t empty—it’s full, like a glass of water just before it spills over. That’s the kind of silence I’ve been chasing, the kind that doesn’t ask for anything, doesn’t demand an answer, doesn’t even whisper a question. It just *is*. And in that silence, words lose their edges. They soften, blur, become something else entirely.

I’ve always been afraid of words. Not the way some people are afraid of spiders or heights—no, this is different. It’s the fear of their power, their ability to wound or heal with the same casual precision. A single word can unravel a life, can stitch one back together. *Sorry.* *Always.* *Never.* *Love.* They’re just sounds, really, vibrations in the air, but they carry the weight of entire universes. And yet, we toss them around like coins, like they’re nothing.

I remember the first time I realized this. I was twelve, sitting in the back of my sixth-grade classroom, watching Mrs. Calloway write on the chalkboard. She was teaching us about metaphors, how words could be bridges, how they could carry meaning from one thing to another. *"The world is a stage,"* she wrote, and I stared at those words until they stopped making sense. The world. A stage. What did that even mean? And then, like a door swinging open, I understood: it didn’t *mean* anything. Not really. It was just a way of seeing, a lens. And suddenly, everything looked different.

That was the day I started collecting words. Not in a notebook, not in a way that anyone could see, but in the quiet corners of my mind. I’d hear a phrase in a song, or read a line in a book, and I’d tuck it away, like a magpie with a shiny thing. *"The moon was a ghostly galleon tossed upon cloudy seas."* *"Hope is the thing with feathers."* *"Do I dare disturb the universe?"* They became my talismans, my secret language. I’d whisper them to myself when I was scared, or lonely, or just trying to make sense of the noise in my head.

But words are tricky. They promise clarity, but they can just as easily obscure. They promise connection, but they can build walls. I learned that the hard way.

There was a boy in high school—let’s call him Daniel. He had a way of making the world feel lighter, like he was carrying a pocketful of helium and letting it leak out in little bursts. We’d sit on the hood of his car after school, passing a bag of sour gummy worms between us, and he’d tell me stories about his childhood, about the time he tried to build a rocket out of cardboard and fireworks, about the summer he spent working at his uncle’s farm and learned how to milk a goat. His words were effortless, like breathing. And I loved listening to them.

One day, I worked up the courage to tell him about my word collection. I don’t know why I did it—maybe because I wanted to share something that felt like *me*, or maybe because I was tired of carrying it alone. I told him about the metaphors, about the way certain phrases made my chest ache, about how I’d lie in bed at night and string words together like beads on a necklace, just to see how they’d look.

He listened, his head tilted to the side, his expression unreadable. And then he laughed.

Not a mean laugh. Not cruel. Just… confused. *"That’s weird,"* he said. *"Why would you do that?"*

I felt the words shrivel up inside me, like paper held too close to a flame. I shrugged, forced a laugh of my own. *"I don’t know. It’s just… something I do."*

But it wasn’t *just* something I did. It was something I *was*. And in that moment, I realized how fragile that was. How easily it could be dismissed, or mocked, or—worst of all—ignored.

I stopped telling people about my words after that. I buried them deeper, let them grow tangled roots in the dark. And for a while, I convinced myself that was fine. That I didn’t need them. That I could live without them.

But words don’t work like that. They don’t stay buried. They seep out, like ink through paper, staining everything. They find their way into your dreams, your jokes, the way you describe the color of the sky. They become the scaffolding of your thoughts, the architecture of your mind. And when you try to silence them, they don’t disappear—they just get louder.

I’m thirty now, and I still collect words. I still whisper them to myself in the dark. But I’ve learned a few things along the way.

I’ve learned that words are not just tools—they’re living things. They evolve, they shift, they take on new meanings depending on who’s holding them. *"Home"* means something different to a refugee than it does to someone who’s never left their hometown. *"Freedom"* sounds different in a prison cell than it does in a classroom. Words are not neutral. They carry history, bias, pain, joy. They are never just *words*.

I’ve learned that silence is its own kind of language. There’s the silence of comfort, the kind that settles between two people who know each other so well they don’t need to fill the space. And then there’s the silence of absence, the kind that screams. I’ve sat in both. I’ve learned to listen to them.

I’ve learned that some words are too heavy to say out loud. *"I’m sorry."* *"I miss you."* *"I was wrong."* They get stuck in your throat, like fishbones. And sometimes, the only way to dislodge them is to write them down, to let them exist outside of you, where they can’t hurt as much.

I’ve learned that the right word, at the right time, can change everything. A *"yes"* when you’re afraid. A *"no"* when you’re drowning. A *"me too"* when you feel alone. Words can be lifelines. They can be anchors. They can be wings.

And I’ve learned that the fear of words—the fear of saying the wrong thing, of not being understood, of being too much or not enough—is universal. We’re all just stumbling through this, trying to find the right combination of sounds to explain ourselves, to connect, to be seen.

So here’s what I know, in this moment, in this silence before dawn:

Words are not the enemy. They are not the problem. The problem is the way we use them—or don’t. The problem is the way we let them divide us, or the way we hoard them, or the way we pretend they don’t matter.

But they do matter. They matter more than we realize.

And maybe, if we’re lucky, we’ll find the right ones. Maybe we’ll string them together in a way that makes sense, that builds something beautiful, that lasts. Or maybe we won’t. Maybe we’ll just keep stumbling, keep searching, keep whispering into the dark.

But that’s okay. Because the words are still there. Waiting. Always waiting.
